definition: Full roof tear off removes every existing layer of roof covering, underlayment, and flashing down to the bare deck before a new roof system is installed. It exposes the sheathing for inspection and repair, unlike a recover that leaves the old covering in place. A full tear-off becomes the code-mandated path once a deck is water-soaked or deteriorated, the covering is wood shake or tile, or the roof already carries two or more layers, per N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4.

costRanges.item: Old-roof removal (the tear-off labor a recover skips)
costRanges.range: $1–$5 per square foot by material weight ($1–$3 for shingles, $2–$5 for heavier slate or tile)

costRanges.source: HomeAdvisor and Modernize NJ cost data (per gold)

costRanges.range: $220–$580 per week for a 10-yard container and $280–$699 per week for a 20-yard container on a large roof

signs: A roof already carrying 2 or more layers of covering mandates a full tear-off, because N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 and IRC Section R908.3.1.1 prohibit a recover where 2 or more applications already exist, leaving complete removal the only code-compliant path, per the NJ Uniform Construction Code.

A water-soaked or deteriorated roof deck mandates a full tear-off, because N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 bars a recover over a deck that is not an adequate base, and a recover hides the rot a tear-off repairs, per the Asphalt Roofing Manufacturers Association and InterNACHI.

A wood-shake, slate, clay, cement, or asbestos-cement tile covering mandates a full tear-off under N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4, the NJ Rehabilitation Subcode condition that expressly adds wood shake to the IRC Section R908.3.1.1 removal list, per the NJ Uniform Construction Code.

Daylight visible through the roof deck from inside the attic indicates a direct breach in the sheathing, a failing-deck sign that points to tear-off and deck replacement rather than a surface patch, per InterNACHI.

Soft, spongy, or sagging sheathing felt underfoot or seen between rafters indicates moisture-rotted decking that cannot hold a roofing nail, the structural condition ARMA nail-application guidance ties to required sheathing replacement.

Delaminated plywood or swollen OSB edges on the deck underside indicate irreversible saturation, because OSB once water-soaked swells at the edges and delaminates rather than drying out, per InterNACHI.

A roof past its material lifespan with widespread granule loss favors a full tear-off, because 3-tab asphalt lasts about 20 years and architectural asphalt about 30 years, per the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart, beyond which a recover delivers a shortened service life over an aged base.
selectionCriteria: Verify the contractor holds a New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor registration under N.J.S.A. 56:8-136, with its 13VH registration number printed on the contract and advertising per N.J.S.A. 56:8-144 — a registration, not a roofing license, since New Jersey issues no roofing license.
Confirm at least $500,000 per-occurrence commercial general liability coverage required of a registered NJ HIC under N.J.S.A. 56:8-142, verified by a current certificate of insurance.
Require a written contract for any home-improvement work over $500 under N.J.A.C. 13:45A-16.2, with the total price, start and completion dates, and a description of the work.

Require an itemized written estimate that breaks out the tear-off labor, disposal, deck-repair allowance, materials, and the permit path — separate from the detached one- and two-family ordinary-maintenance exemption under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7.
Require a documented deck assessment that counts the existing covering layers and checks the deck against the N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 mandatory-removal conditions before the tear-off quote.

Ask for local Essex County references and confirm the contractor handles the deck-repair supplement honestly — disclosing re-decking cost when tear-off exposes rotted sheathing rather than burying it.

If the tear-off follows storm or fire damage and runs through insurance, the homeowner or a licensed public adjuster files and negotiates the claim under N.J.S.A. 17:22B — a roofing contractor documents the damage and meets the adjuster on site but cannot legally waive the deductible, promise a free roof, or guarantee claim approval.

technicalFacts.fact: N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 (NJ Rehabilitation Subcode) requires complete removal of the existing covering, with no recover-over, in 3 conditions: a water-soaked or deteriorated deck, a wood-shake/slate/clay/cement/asbestos-cement tile covering, or a roof already carrying 2 or more layers; it adds wood shake to the IRC Section R908.3.1.1 model removal list.
technicalFacts.source: N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4; ICC IRC Section R908.3.1.1; NJ Uniform Construction Code (per gold + fact pack)

technicalFacts.fact: A maximum of two layers of covering is permitted — no third layer; a recover is prohibited where 2 or more applications already exist, and a future re-roof over two layers then requires tearing off both at higher cost.
technicalFacts.source: ICC IRC R908.3.1.1; N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 (per fact pack)

technicalFacts.fact: A tear-off lets a roofer inspect the roof deck, repair any damage, and improve deck attachment to the structure, while a recover leaves the underlying layers difficult to inspect so rot and water damage go uncaught.
technicalFacts.source: Asphalt Roofing Manufacturers Association (ARMA); InterNACHI (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: Roofing nails must penetrate at least ¾ inch into the deck to grip the fastener, so sheathing that has rotted soft, delaminated, or swollen cannot hold a nail and is replaced; saturated OSB swells at the edges and delaminates irreversibly, so it is re-decked rather than dried.
technicalFacts.source: ARMA nail-application guidance; InterNACHI sheathing inspection (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: A self-adhering ice barrier is required from the eave to a point at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line in ice-prone regions like Essex County, per the IRC ice-barrier provision (R905.1.2) as enforced under N.J.A.C. 5:23.
technicalFacts.source: International Residential Code R905.1.2; N.J.A.C. 5:23 (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: A complete tear-off and replacement of the roof covering on a detached one- and two-family dwelling counts as ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and requires no construction permit, no inspection, and no notice to the construction official; a commercial roof or a structural change to rafters or trusses does require a permit, and the exemption does not authorize a non-compliant recover.
technicalFacts.source: N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7; NJ Uniform Construction Code (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: A second overlay layer adds roughly 2 to 4.5 pounds per square foot of dead load across the deck and rafters, so a multi-layer roof at the 2-layer maximum carries the full weight a tear-off removes.
technicalFacts.source: Dumpsters.com Shingle Weight Calculator / Sourgum (converted); Angi (per gold + fact pack)

technicalFacts.fact: Installing the new cover to manufacturer specification preserves the manufacturer material warranty covering factory defects, which is separate from the contractor's written workmanship warranty backing the labor.

Replace vs repair thresholds: replace when damage exceeds 25–30% of the roof area or one repair approaches 50% of replacement cost, repair when damage stays localized on an asphalt roof under 10–15 years old; these are contractor-consensus thresholds, and tear-off becomes the code-mandated path once the deck is water-soaked or the roof carries 2 layers.

sources: ICC International Residential Code Section R908.3.1.1
ICC International Residential Code R905.1.2 (ice barrier)

defabToKill.fix: Correct the code value: current 2021 IECC attic insulation for Climate Zone 4-5 is R-60 (R-49 is the raised-heel exception only). defabToKill.fix: Delete — unsourced and off-topic for a tear-off; no gold or fact-pack support for tear-off rebates.

defabToKill.fix: Wrong for 1-2 family homes. Per N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7, a complete tear-off and replacement of the roof covering on a detached one- and two-family dwelling is ordinary maintenance requiring NO construction permit, no inspection, and no notice; only a commercial roof or a structural change to rafters/trusses triggers a permit.

parentDebtToAvoid: Do not reproduce the "NJ HIC Licensed" credential chip from the gold credentialsHighlight — use "registered NJ HIC" / registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor; New Jersey issues no roofing license.

Do not frame Newark Quality Roofing as GAF / CertainTeed / Owens Corning certified, Master Elite, SELECT ShingleMaster, or Preferred; brands may be named only as external warranty/data/guidance sources (e.g., Owens Corning warranty guidance, GAF TAB-R-145).
Do not state any "licensed" framing for NQR; the credential is NJ HIC registration under N.J.S.A. 56:8-136, not a license.
Do not invent NQR volume claims ("hundreds of tear-offs"); NQR is a registered NJ HIC serving Essex County with no project counts.
Do not present the overlay as equal to a tear-off or assert a Newark/Essex-specific overlay-vs-tear-off price; the cost-delta and lifespan-haircut figures are national (HomeGuide/Angi).

articleAngles.signs: Open with the definitive trigger: a full roof tear-off becomes mandatory the moment N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 conditions appear — a roof already carrying 2 or more layers, a water-soaked or deteriorated deck, or a wood-shake/slate/tile covering — and the deck-failure signs (daylight, soft/spongy wood, sagging, delaminated plywood, swollen OSB per InterNACHI) that an overlay cannot fix. The signs are part code mandate, part observable deck failure.
articleAngles.costGuide: There IS a real whole-job total: a New Jersey roof replacement with tear-off included runs $10,000–$25,000 for a typical home (HomeAdvisor/Modernize), and the tear-off labor itself is $1–$5 per square foot by material weight (HomeGuide). Lead with the whole-job range, then break out the per-sf removal adder, disposal ($220–$699/week dumpster), and the deck-repair allowance ($2–$5/sf re-decking) — all national-sourced, no invented Essex figures.
articleAngles.decision: The single most important thing a homeowner should understand: the New Jersey code limit of two covering layers is the defining decision factor. Once a roof carries two layers or a deck is water-soaked, N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 removes the overlay option entirely — a tear-off is the only code-compliant path — and that is precisely the case where a tear-off pays off, because stripping to the deck is the only way to inspect and repair the sheathing an overlay would bury, per ARMA and InterNACHI.
